newsitem.title: USA: Police hunt for two Texas separatists.
newsitem.headline: Police hunt for two Texas separatists.

text.p: Police scoured a remote west Texas mountain range on Sunday for two escaped, armed separatists a day after their group surrendered at the end of a week-long siege.
Helicopters, at least 20 bloodhounds and two teams of troopers on horseback searched throughout the night for the two men, identified as Richard Keyes and Mike Matson.
"There's no place for them to go," Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox said. "We have the back of the area sealed off. They are in there somewhere."

The two men, both in their early 20s, walked away from the Republic of Texas mountain compound when the separatist group's leader Richard McLaren, his wife and three others put down their guns and surrendered to police forces on Saturday.

Police saw Keyes and Matson escape into the Davis Mountains at around midday on Saturday but did not begin searching for them until four hours later, after the other Republic members had given themselves up, because they did not want to jeopardise the delicate negotiations which eventually brought the surrender of McLaren and his other followers.

Officials said the two men were dressed in camouflage and armed with an assault rifle, a deer-hunting rifle and a 9mm pistol, but rejected suggestions they had moved too slowly and said Keyes and Matson did not pose a serious threat.
Cox said the quantity of explosives and firearms inside the Republic's dilapidated compound demonstrated that ending the siege was more important than chasing the two escapees.
An ordnance team on Sunday exploded a makeshift bomb and police found 40 to 60 pipe bombs stored in a series of makeshift bunkers around the compound, Cox said.
The ragtag militia group also set up a dozen gasoline-filled cannisters rigged to rain down fire on the road leading into the embassy.

McLaren and his other followers, who claim Texas is an independent nation, had vowed to defend their "embassy" compound to the death but surrendered when scores of police surrounded them and prepared to move in.

They were taken to Presidio County Jail in nearby Marfa, Texas, and arraigned on Saturday night. McLaren was jailed without bond and faces state felony charges tied to the kidnapping of two neighbours at the start of the standoff last Sunday, as well as federal contempt of court charges.
His wife Evelyn and the three other Republic members -- Richard "White Eagle" Otto, Karen and Gregg Paulson and Robert Schedit -- were each held on $500,000 bond.
The McLarens spent Saturday night in the same jail cell, a privilege negotiated during the final hours of the siege.

All the prisoners and one of the two escapees could face between five years and 99 years in prison for the state felony charges. Matson faces no charges and police said they did not understand why he chose to flee.

McLaren had been holed up inside his compound for four months after an arrest warrant was issued against him on contempt charges, but the situation only turned dangerous when police arrested a Republic member last Sunday and McLaren retaliated by ordering the kidnapping of two neighbours. They were released 12 hours later in a prisoner exchange.

McLaren finally agreed to turn himself in when Texas Rangers signed off on a "cease-fire agreement" which included recognition of the Republic of Texas and an assurance that McLaren will be given the opportunity to argue before a federal judge in Washington D.C. that there should be a referendum on the issue of Texas independence.
The agreement also allowed the Republic to fly its flag -- a lone yellow star on a blue field -- over the west Texas "embassy," but it was later lowered.
The Republic members face a battery of charges in the siege, which began on Sunday when they took two hostages in retaliation for the arrest by local police of security chief Robert Scheidt.

The Republic of Texas, which claims to have thousands of members and ties to anti-government militia groups, says that Texas' 1845 annexation by the United States was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after it broke from Mexico in an 1836 rebellion McLaren likened to his own.
